claims.text: In-flight oxidation during HVOF spraying can generate oxides in an HEA coating.
Controlled in-flight oxidation produces a uniform dispersion of nanoscale oxide precipitates within the FCC/BCC HEA matrix.
Nano-oxide precipitates pin dislocations in the HEA matrix.
Dislocation pinning by nano-oxides retards creep deformation during continuous high-temperature loading.
The starting coating is an as-sprayed FCC/BCC HEA with low oxide content and limited oxide dispersion resulting from minimal in-flight oxidation.
Changing oxygen partial pressure during HVOF or plasma spraying can tune the amount of in situ oxide formation.
Changing oxygen partial pressure during spraying can tune the spatial uniformity of the oxide dispersion.
Coatings with systematically varied oxide contents should be compared under sustained loading at 750–1000 °C while other processing variables are controlled.
The governing structural mediator is a homogeneous dispersion of in situ nanoscale oxide precipitates.
Nano-oxide particles inhibit both dislocation climb and dislocation glide during high-temperature creep.
Nano-oxide strengthening increases the threshold stress for creep activation and delays plastic deformation.
An optimized uniform oxide dispersion will produce a lower creep strain rate than the minimally oxidized baseline.
An optimized uniform oxide dispersion will produce a higher creep threshold than the minimally oxidized baseline.
An optimized uniform oxide dispersion will extend time to failure relative to the minimally oxidized baseline.
Measured oxide dispersion will correlate positively with creep resistance.
The proposed oxide-pinning mechanism is effective under sustained stress between 750 °C and 1000 °C.
Excessive or inhomogeneous oxidation can cause brittleness or reduce coating toughness.
The magnitude of creep improvement depends on oxide-particle size, spatial distribution, and volume fraction.
TEM and SEM/EDS measurements, constant-load creep tests, and local mechanical-property tests can compare coatings made at different oxygen partial pressures.

Failure of coatings with increased, uniformly dispersed oxide content to show a statistically significant creep-rate reduction or longer time to failure relative to baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
